x.ASV: And he said unto me, Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak with thee.
x.Darby: And he said unto me, Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak with thee.
x.KJV: And he said unto me, Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee.
x.YLT: It is the appearance of the likeness of the honour of Jehovah, and I see, and fall on my face, and I hear a voice speaking, and He saith unto me, `Son of man, stand on thy feet, and I speak with thee.'

nt: The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh who is the one whom Ezekiel saw sitting on the throne, as described in the previous chapter. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Then the one who was seated on the throne said to me]

Yahweh is using **Son of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “human being.” See the Introduction to Ezekiel for more information on this form of address. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

t: and/ it made stand up/ me

x.ASV: And the Spirit entered into me when he spake unto me, and set me upon my feet; and I heard him that spake unto me.
x.Darby: And the Spirit entered into me when he spoke unto me, and set me upon my feet; and I heard him that spoke unto me.
x.KJV: And the spirit entered into me when he spake unto me, and set me upon my feet, that I heard him that spake unto me.
x.YLT: And there doth come into me a spirit, when He hath spoken unto me, and it causeth me to stand on my feet, and I hear Him who is speaking unto me.

nt: By **it made me stand on my feet**, Ezekiel means that the Holy Spirit gave him the strength to rise, since he had fallen facedown to the ground in awe of the glory of Yahweh [1:28](../01/28.md) and could not stand up on his own. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the Spirit gave me the strength to stand up]

The implication is that the one who was **speaking** to Ezekiel was the one whom he saw sitting on the throne. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers as in the UST.

x.ASV: And he said unto me, Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to nations that are rebellious, which have rebelled against me: they and their fathers have transgressed against me even unto this very day.
x.Darby: And he said unto me, Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to nations that are rebellious, which have rebelled against me: they and their fathers have transgressed against me unto this very day;
x.KJV: And he said unto me, Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to a rebellious nation that hath rebelled against me: they and their fathers have transgressed against me, even unto this very day.
x.YLT: And He saith unto Me, `Son of man, I am sending thee unto the sons of Israel, unto nations who are rebels, who have rebelled against Me; they and their fathers have transgressed against Me, unto this self-same day.

nt: Yahweh is using the present tense to describe something that is going to happen in the immediate future. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use the future tense. Alternate translation: [I will send you to the sons of Israel]

Yahweh is speaking of the Israelites as if they were the **sons** of their ancestor Jacob, who was also named **Israel.** Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the people of Israel]

Yahweh is speaking of the tribes of Israel as if they were **nations**, using a term that ordinarily describes the foreign peoples who do not worship him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to a rebellious people who behave like they do not belong to me]

Yahweh is speaking of the earlier generations of the people of Israel as if they were the **fathers** of the current generation. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the generations before them]

Yahweh is using **up to the bone of this day** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to this very day.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [right up to the present time]

x.ASV: And the children are impudent and stiffhearted: I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah.
x.Darby: and these children are impudent and hard-hearted: I am sending thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah.
x.KJV: For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God.
x.YLT: And the sons are brazen-faced and hard-hearted to whom I am sending thee, and thou hast said unto them: Thus said the Lord Jehovah:

nt: The word **sons** refers back to previous verse where “sons of Israel” meant the people of Israel.

The expressions **hard of face** and **strong of heart** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [extremely obstinate]

Yahweh is using **hard of face** as a common expression of the culture to mean that they were unyielding and showing willful resistance to him. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are unyielding]

Yahweh is using **strong of heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “stubbornly determined to have their own way.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and determined to have their own way]

Yahweh is instructing Ezekiel, **and you will say to them, ‘Thus says the Lord Yahweh.’** to indicate that what he is telling Ezekiel to say comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating the authoritative source of direct quotations in your language.

x.ASV: And they, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear (for they are a rebellious house), yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them.
x.Darby: And they, whether they will hear or whether they will forbear — for they are a rebellious house — yet shall they know that there hath been a prophet among them.
x.KJV: And they, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house,) yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them.
x.YLT: and they--whether they hear, or whether they forbear, for a rebellious house they are --have known that a prophet hath been in their midst.

nt: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [whether they listen to you or whether they refuse to listen to you]
Here, **listen** means to intentionally hear and obey. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [whether they listen and obey what you tell them]

Yahweh is using **house of** as a common expression of the culture to indicate people with a certain characteristic. In this case, they have the characteristic of being rebellious. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they are a rebellious people]

The implication is that the **prophet** whom Yahweh is describing is Ezekiel himself and that the people will know that his message is from Yahweh himself. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [but they will know that you, my prophet, are in their midst]

x.ASV: And thou, son of man, be not afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns are with thee, and thou dost dwell among scorpions: be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, though they are a rebellious house.
x.Darby: And thou, son of man, be not afraid of them, and be not afraid of their words; for briars and thorns are with thee, and thou dwellest among scorpions: be not afraid of their words, and be not dismayed at their faces; for they are a rebellious house.
x.KJV: And thou, son of man, be not afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns be with thee, and thou dost dwell among scorpions: be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house.
x.YLT: `And thou, son of man, thou art not afraid of them, yea, of their words thou art not afraid, for briers and thorns are with thee, and near scorpions thou art dwelling, of their words thou art not afraid, and of their faces thou art not affrighted, for they are a rebellious house,

nt: The phrase translated as **you shall not fear** is an imperative, but it communicates reassurance rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate reassurance for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates reassurance. Alternate translation: [you have no need to fear because of them]

Yahweh is speaking of the people to whom he is sending Ezekiel as if they were **briers and thorns**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [hurtful people]

The terms **briers** and **thorns** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [sharp thorns]

Yahweh is speaking of the people among whom Ezekiel would live as if they were **scorpions**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you are dwelling among people who hurt you like scorpions]

Here the phrase **from their faces** could: (1) represent “from their presence.” Alternate translation: [and from their presence you shall not be afraid] or (2) be a common expression of the culture that means “on their account” or “on their behalf,” Alternate translation: [and because of them you shall not be dismayed]
See how you translated this same phrase, “a house of rebellion,” in [the previous verse](../02/05.md).

x.ASV: And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear; for they are most rebellious.
x.Darby: And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear or whether they will forbear; for they are rebellious.
x.KJV: And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear: for they are most rebellious.
x.YLT: And thou hast spoken My words unto them, whether they hear or whether they forbear, for they are rebellious.

nt: See how you translated these same phrases in [verse 5](../02/05.md). Alternate translation: [whether they listen and obey my words or whether they refuse to listen to and obey my words]

Here, **a rebellion** represents “people who rebel.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [because they are people who rebel]

x.ASV: But thou, son of man, hear what I say unto thee; be not thou rebellious like that rebellious house: open thy mouth, and eat that which I give thee.
x.Darby: And thou, son of man, hear what I say unto thee; be not thou rebellious like that rebellious house: open thy mouth, and eat that I give thee.
x.KJV: But thou, son of man, hear what I say unto thee; Be not thou rebellious like that rebellious house: open thy mouth, and eat that I give thee.
x.YLT: `And thou, son of man, hear that which I am speaking unto thee: Thou art not rebellious like the rebellious house, open thy mouth, and eat that which I am giving unto thee.'

nt: See how you translated the similar phrase, “a house of rebellion” in [verse 5](../02/05.md). Alternate translation: [like these rebellious people]
פְּצֵ֣ה פִ֔י⁠ךָ וֶ⁠אֱכֹ֕ל אֵ֥ת אֲשֶׁר־אֲנִ֖י נֹתֵ֥ן אֵלֶֽי⁠ךָ

Eating what Yahweh was giving him would be a symbolic action by which Ezekiel would show that he was receiving Yahweh’s message into himself so that he could speak it to the people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in a footnote.

x.ASV: And when I looked, behold, a hand was put forth unto me; and, lo, a roll of a book was therein;
x.Darby: And I looked, and behold, a hand was put forth toward me; and behold, a roll of a book therein.
x.KJV: And when I looked, behold, an hand was sent unto me; and, lo, a roll of a book was therein;
x.YLT: And I look, and lo, a hand is sent forth unto me, and lo, in it a roll of a book,

nt: Ezekiel is using the term **behold** to focus his readers’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Ezekiel uses this term twice in this verse. Alternate translation: [and there, right before me, a hand was being sent to me. And suddenly, I saw that it was holding]

The expression **was being sent** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he was extending a hand toward me]

x.ASV: and he spread it before me: and it was written within and without; and there were written therein lamentations, and mourning, and woe.
x.Darby: And he spread it out before me; and it was written within and without; and there were written in it lamentations, and mourning, and woe.
x.KJV: And he spread it before me; and it was written within and without: and there was written therein lamentations, and mourning, and woe.
x.YLT: and He spreadeth it before me, and it is written in front and behind, and written on it are lamentations, and mourning, and woe!

nt: The pronoun **he** refers to the one who was speaking to Ezekiel, and the pronoun **it** refers to the scroll. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the one who was speaking to me spread the scroll out before me]

The expression **was written** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and it had writing on its front and back]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **laments**, **mourning**, and **woe**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [words that expressed sorrow and mourning and words about suffering]
